name: Nikhil Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. As long as my name's not on it, fine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you walk me through a normal working day, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a soft drinks and bottled water warehouse on the bypass, the regional one that supplies the corner shops and the cash-and-carry. Cases of cola, crates of water, 12 kilos each, stacked onto pallets by hand. Six in the morning till half two, and you're done in by lunchtime in summer when everyone wants water. My dad did the same kind of work for thirty years at the old brewery depot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the lads, and I like that it's honest work, you lift, you earn. What wears me out is the summer rush and the pay, which is the bottom end. I'm getting married next summer to Sana, my fiancée, and I live at my parents' to save, but with the wedding costs I've got almost nothing put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it was all talk from people in offices. At work I'd say it in the canteen. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing new, which is fine but not great. The wedding is about £9,000 between both families and my share is a lot for my wage. The job's safe, but it doesn't pay enough for a man starting a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, do every bit of overtime in the summer rush, that's an extra £300 some months. I'd keep living at my parents' till the wedding. And I'd ask my uncle about weekend work in his tyre shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mainly about the wedding money. Not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your family feel about the wedding costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad says don't borrow, ever. My mum says the family will help. I want to do it myself, that's how I was brought up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever think about a different job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I know this work. My dad did it, I do it. I'd rather get better at it than start from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office lot will get it first, the people who never lifted a case. I'd say good luck to a robot picking a crate of water. At work I'd laugh about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've seen the automatic pallet wrappers and the stacking machines at the big drinks factory. Cases of cola are all the same shape, which is exactly what a robot likes. I think in a few years they'll come for the pallet building, and I'm not a computer person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work hard so I'm the one they keep. I'd keep the overtime. I'd talk to my dad and uncle about what to do if it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not much I can do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd work hard to be kept. Would learning the new machines help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I don't trust myself with screens and settings. I'd rather lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change the wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The wedding is happening. Maybe smaller, maybe fewer guests, but it's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and the government needs to stop companies throwing people out all at once. Not handouts, but proper jobs, apprenticeships. I'd say it at the mosque too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be finished at the warehouse by 2031. The office goes in 2028, then the stacking robots. I'd be married with no savings and maybe a baby on the way. I don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, that's the honest truth. I'd keep working. I'd ask my uncle if I could work at the tyre shop full time, but he can't pay much. I'd ask the mosque if anyone knows of jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like the floor's dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: There are three years before the robots arrive. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should. But I don't know what to do with three years. I'm not a student.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my fiancée I'll look after us, because that's my job. But I wouldn't know how. Sana would see through that, she always does.

say: I'd say the **government** must stop firms throwing everyone out at once.
I'd ask for **apprenticeships**, not handouts, at work and at the mosque.
think: I'd be **finished** at the warehouse by 2031.
Married with **no savings** and maybe a baby, I don't know what I'd do.
do: Keep **working** at the warehouse as long as possible.
Ask his uncle about **full-time** work at the tyre shop.
Ask people at the **mosque** about jobs.
S2.quote: I'd tell my fiancée I'll look after us, because that's my job. But I wouldn't know how.
fieldNote: He has **no plan** and says so honestly.
The **three-year gap** doesn't help because he doesn't know how to use it.
Leans on **family and mosque** networks, not government handouts.

steps.text: Keep stacking drinks pallets for as long as the job lasts
Ask his uncle for full-time work at the tyre shop
Ask people at the mosque about job openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to sort out apprenticeships for people like me. I'd say the companies should train their own. I'd say it at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the office, eight for the robots. I'd be 35, maybe with a couple of kids. I'd want a trade by then, something with my hands. Like my uncle, tyres and brakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle to teach me tyres and brakes on weekends. I'd try to save a bit after the wedding, maybe £50 a month. I'd keep the warehouse job till the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed but less. At least I can see a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go to college for the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to. I'd rather learn a trade from my uncle, that's how my family does it. He learned from his own father in the same shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have them. Maybe wait a year or two. That's Sana's call as much as mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, people should stop panicking. I'd say work hard and learn a trade. At work and with family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and the robots in 2039. I'd be 40 with kids at school. I'd want to be in the tyre shop by then, maybe running it when my uncle retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the warehouse job for now, because it's steady and it's near home. I'd learn tyres at my uncle's on Saturdays, starting with the simple jobs like puncture repairs. After the wedding I'd put £50 a month away and try not to touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more about the wedding money than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn a trade, and something with a computer too. I don't want my kids stuck like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see yourself as stuck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I've always done what I know. Ten years is time to change, but I'd still have to actually do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no plan and a new wife. What would help is a proper apprenticeship for grown men, paid, at a real business, not a classroom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about family. Most people round here would lean on family before the government. That's how it should be, but families can only carry so much.

headlineQuote: Most people round here would lean on family before the government. That's how it should be, but families can only carry so much.
portrait: **Nikhil** is 27 and stacks drinks pallets at a regional warehouse, like his dad did at a brewery depot.
He lives with his parents and is saving for a **wedding** next summer with almost nothing put by.
He's **traditional** and leans on family and the mosque rather than government.
He avoids **screens** and dreads a fast timeline with no plan.
He swings from uneasy to **panicked** at AGI by 2028, with a family trade as his hope.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no **plan** and a new wife.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** for adults at a real business, not a classroom.
